narrative:
The model determined that you have an 86% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score of 24 was by far the strongest influence, pulling the prediction heavily toward failure. Compared with the average of 37 among accepted students, this score signaled a significant gap in the skills the bar exam tests. Your third-year class ranking came next; placing in the third decile rather than the fifth-decile average of accepted students added further weight toward a fail prediction. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.4, well below the 3.23 average of successful applicants, provided additional downward pressure.

None of these features pointed in a positive direction. Each one reinforced the others, creating a consistent picture of elevated risk that the model could not overlook.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, improve your study habits to raise your class ranking, and consider post-baccalaureate coursework to demonstrate that your undergraduate grades do not reflect your current ability. Once you can show clear progress in these core academic indicators, reapply. Many students improve these metrics and go on to pass the bar successfully.
